name: Yom Kippur (The Day of Atonement)
description: The holiest day in the Jewish calendar — fasting, repentance, and atonement.
biblicalBasis: Leviticus 16 describes the ritual in detail: the high priest changes into white linen garments, sacrifices a bull for himself, chooses two goats — one for the Lord (a sin offering) and one for Azazel (the scapegoat sent into the wilderness bearing the people's sins). He enters the Most Holy Place with incense and blood, sprinkling the blood on the mercy seat of the ark of the covenant. Leviticus 23:26-32: "You shall fast and humble yourselves... anyone who does not humble themselves shall be cut off."
significance: Yom Kippur is the only day the high priest entered the Most Holy Place — God's direct presence. The book of Hebrews interprets this as a foreshadowing of Christ: "Christ came as high priest... He entered once for all into the heavenly sanctuary, not with the blood of goats and calves, but with his own blood, thus obtaining eternal redemption" (Heb 9:11-12). The scapegoat carries the people's sin away — a picture of substitutionary atonement.
liturgicalContext: Observed on the 10th of Tishri. A 25-hour fast without food or drink. The Kol Nidre prayer on the evening before. Five services throughout the day. The concluding ceremony, Ne'ila (the gates are closed), culminates in one long shofar blast. White garments as a symbol of purity.
history: In temple times, Yom Kippur was the most dramatic and dangerous service — the high priest could die in the Most Holy Place if the ritual was not performed correctly. After the temple's destruction, prayer and fasting replaced sacrifices. Rabbinic tradition: "For offenses against God, Yom Kippur atones. For offenses against fellow humans, it does not atone until one has made peace with the person they have wronged" (Mishnah Yoma 8:9).
otConnections: Leviticus 16 in its entirety is the foundation. Leviticus 23:26-32 regarding fasting. Isaiah 58:1-12 about true fasting. The book of Jonah is read during the afternoon service — God's willingness to forgive, even Nineveh. Ezekiel 36:25-26: "I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean... I will give you a new heart."
